rules.title: Character Set
rules.checks: Checks that the file contains only plain ASCII characters (codes 0-127). Extended ASCII (128-255, e.g. the degree symbol) is tolerated but only flagged for information; characters above 255 (smart quotes, em-dashes) and a byte-order mark (BOM) are hard errors. A finding means a non-ASCII character or BOM was found at the reported position. To fix: replace smart quotes/dashes with plain ASCII equivalents, or let the validator strip a BOM automatically.

observations.note: The validator deliberately tolerates extended ASCII (128-255) as info-only and only errors above 255, matching python-ags4's leniency rather than the strict spec which requires 0-127. So a degree symbol will not block your file.

If the file is not valid UTF-8, bad bytes are replaced with the Unicode replacement character (U+FFFD) rather than rejecting the whole file outright; those replaced bytes then surface as Rule 1 errors.

rules.title: Data Groups and Data Rows
rules.checks: Checks that every GROUP in the file has at least one DATA row. A finding means a group has only header rows (HEADING/UNIT/TYPE) and no actual data. To fix: add the missing data rows, or remove the empty group if it is not needed.

observations.note: A PROJ or TRAN group with zero data rows is reported twice: once here (general empty-group rule) and once by Rule 13/14 (specific cardinality). This double-report is expected; both validators behave this way.

A HEADING, UNIT, TYPE or DATA row appearing before any GROUP row belongs to no group, and is reported here, line-located. python-ags4's parser raises on the same row instead, so it produces a traceback and no report at all — you get the whole picture from this file, including the structural fault, rather than stopping at the first one.

rules.title: Line Termination
rules.checks: Checks that every line ends with a carriage-return + line-feed pair (CRLF, \r\n). A finding means a line ended with a bare LF, or the final line had no terminator. To fix: this is corrected automatically by normalising all line endings to CRLF (common when a file was saved on macOS/Linux).

rules.title: Group Header Structure
rules.checks: Checks that every group has a complete, correctly ordered header: the UNIT row must immediately follow the HEADING row, and the TYPE row must immediately follow the UNIT row. A finding means a UNIT or TYPE row is missing or out of position. To fix: add the missing row or reorder so the sequence is HEADING, UNIT, TYPE.

observations.note: A completely missing HEADING row is reported under Rule 4 (field count), not here, even though the spec prose hints it belongs to 2b. This is intentional to match python-ags4's attribution.
Groups that lack a HEADING row are still fully validated by this validator; python-ags4 may under-report on such groups, so you may see findings here that the older tool would miss.

rules.title: Data Descriptors
rules.checks: Checks that every non-blank line starts with one of the five valid descriptors: GROUP, HEADING, UNIT, TYPE, or DATA. A finding means a line begins with something else (a stray value, a typo, or text that is not a proper AGS line). To fix: correct the first field to a valid descriptor or remove the stray line.

rules.title: Field Count and GROUP Row Format
rules.checks: Checks field counts per row: a GROUP row must have exactly two fields (the descriptor plus the 4-letter group name), and every HEADING/UNIT/TYPE/DATA row must have the same number of fields as the HEADING row. A finding means a row has too few or too many fields (often a missing comma, an extra comma, or a ragged DATA row). To fix: align the offending row's field count to the HEADING row.

observations.note: In python-ags4 an unquoted DATA field is reported as a Rule 4 field-count problem rather than a Rule 5 quoting problem; this validator may instead attribute it to Rule 5. The total set of findings matches, but the rule label on this specific defect can differ.
The underlying native parser is lenient (it can merge duplicate GROUPs and pad ragged DATA rows), but a strict pre-check mimics python-ags4's hard-fail so behaviour matches the older tool.

rules.title: Quoted Fields
rules.checks: Checks that every field is wrapped in double quotes and that any literal double-quote inside a field is escaped by doubling it (""). A finding means a field is unquoted or has an unescaped/unbalanced quote. To fix: wrap the field in quotes and double any embedded quote characters.

observations.note: python-ags4 skips the enclosure check on DATA rows and reports unquoted DATA fields as Rule 4 instead. This validator may report them here under Rule 5; the same defect is caught either way.

rules.title: Embedded Carriage Returns
rules.checks: Checks that no carriage-return (CR) character appears inside a row's content; the only legitimate CR is part of the line terminator. A finding means a stray CR was found mid-row. To fix: the embedded CR is deleted automatically.

observations.note: This check is effectively a no-op in python-ags4 (a known upstream bug), even though the spec forbids CR/LF inside quoted fields. This validator implements the real check, so it can catch embedded CRs the older tool silently passed.

rules.title: Heading Order and Duplicates
rules.checks: Checks that a HEADING row has no duplicate field names and that the headings appear in the same relative order as the AGS dictionary (or the file's own DICT group for user-defined headings). A finding means either a repeated heading or headings listed out of order. To fix: duplicates can be renamed automatically (to X_1, X_2, ...); ordering issues must be corrected by hand by reordering the columns.

observations.note: python-ags4 can crash (IndexError) on duplicate headings when its rename option is turned off; this validator guards against that and reports cleanly instead of failing.
The no-duplicate-headings requirement is inferred from the spec rather than stated explicitly. Both tools enforce it; this validator attributes it to Rule 7.
There is no separate DICT-order check (Rule 18a). Dictionary ordering is enforced indirectly here (heading order against the merged dictionary) and by Rule 11 for record links.

rules.title: Typed Values
rules.checks: Checks that every data value matches the format declared in its TYPE row and is consistent with its UNIT. Covers decimal places (nDP), scientific notation (nSCI), significant figures (nSF), dates/times (DT), elapsed time (T), numeric (U), yes/no (YN), degrees-minutes-seconds (DMS), and ID uniqueness. A finding means a value is malformed or wrongly precise for its declared type. To fix: numeric cells (nDP/nSCI/nSF) are reformatted automatically to the declared precision when the cell is a valid number; other type errors (bad dates, non-numeric text, etc.) must be corrected by hand.

observations.note: ID-uniqueness is reported under both Rule 8 (matching python-ags4's attribution) and Rule 10a (the correct relational home), so a non-unique ID may appear twice.

Date/time and elapsed-time values are validated with a different engine (chrono) than python-ags4 (pandas), but behave the same for every UNIT shape in the AGS dictionary. For UNIT shapes the dictionary doesn't recognise, this validator only does a lenient structural check instead of attempting a full parse.
TYPE classification uses exact matching rather than substring matching, which is more robust; conformant data sees no behavioural difference.
Significant-figure (nSF) formatting was matched to python-ags4 by observed behaviour (clean-room), not by copying its source.
An empty DT (date/time) UNIT is now flagged, matching python-ags4. A non-empty but unrecognised UNIT stays lenient (see O-12).

Date/time values are bounded to the pandas Timestamp range (1677-09-21 to 2262-04-11); values outside that window are flagged, closing a range gap that the date engine difference (O-12) otherwise missed.

python-ags4 hard-codes ISO-8601 and rejects non-ISO date UNITs such as dd/mm/yyyy; the spec actually permits the format declared in the UNIT row, so this validator honours the declared format. A date that python-ags4 rejected may validate cleanly here.

The count in a numeric TYPE — the n in 3DP, 3SF, 3SCI — is read from the file's own TYPE row and used as a width when a value is rendered. It is clamped here before it is used. Real AGS types are single-digit, so nothing legitimate is affected; the clamp exists because a corrupt or crafted count reaches the formatter before any rule has vetted the TYPE, and python-ags4 reads it uncapped.

Both validators flag an out-of-range or fractional 0DP cell here, identically — this rule is not where the two differ. They differ afterwards, when the string is CONVERTED to a number: a value too large for a 64-bit integer becomes Null here, where python-ags4's conversion keeps full precision. So a cell can be flagged by both and still read back differently.

rules.title: Dictionary Headings
rules.checks: Checks that every heading used in the file is defined either in the standard AGS dictionary or in the file's own DICT group. A finding means a heading is unknown (often a typo or an undeclared user-defined field). To fix: correct the spelling, or declare the user-defined heading in a DICT group.

observations.note: Which dictionary edition your file is judged against is resolved per file from its TRAN_AGS value, not fixed: all five AGS4 editions are bundled, and an explicit edition option overrides the file's own declaration. So a heading flagged here is one that is absent from THAT edition - check the file's TRAN_AGS before treating it as a typo. The resolution has deliberate rules: bare '4.0' maps to the newest 4.0.x patch, bare '4' to the 4.0 line, an AGS 3.x value is a hard error rather than a silent fallback, and anything missing or unrecognised falls back to 4.1.1 - the same edition python-ags4 falls back to.

rules.title: KEY Field Uniqueness
rules.checks: Checks that the dictionary-defined KEY fields are present in every group and that no two rows in a group share the same combination of KEY values. A finding means a required KEY column is missing or two rows have an identical KEY tuple (a duplicate record). To fix: supply the missing KEY column or make the duplicated rows unique.

observations.note: ID/KEY uniqueness is also reported under Rule 8, so the same duplicate may show up under both rules.
Rules 10a/10b/10c intentionally overlap with Rules 8/13/14; this is deliberate spec layering, not a defect, so some findings appear under more than one rule.

If you validated with a custom dictionary as an OVERLAY, watch for an override warning alongside any finding here. An overlay that demotes a standard KEY heading changes what uniqueness means for that group, so this rule can start answering differently about rows nobody edited. python-ags4 cannot report this: its custom dictionary replaces the standard one outright, leaving nothing to compare an override against.

rules.title: REQUIRED Field Non-Emptiness
rules.checks: Checks that every dictionary-defined REQUIRED field is present and non-empty in each DATA row. A finding means a mandatory field was left blank. To fix: fill in the missing value.

observations.note: Rule 12 (null entries) is defined only as a pointer to this rule and emits nothing itself, so all empty-required-field findings land here under Rule 10b.

A blank TRAN_AGS is reported here, once, and nowhere else. python-ags4 adds a second finding on the same cell saying the edition was not recognised — but only if you asked for the FYI tier, so its default run reports the blank without ever saying which dictionary it then used. That fact is on the report itself here, as the dictionary version and how it was resolved, shown on every run.

rules.title: Parent-Child Linkage
rules.checks: Checks that each row in a child group has a matching parent row in its parent group (per the dictionary) by matching KEY fields. A finding means a child record references a parent that does not exist (an orphan). Top-level groups with no parent (PROJ, TRAN, LOCA, etc.) are exempt. To fix: add the missing parent row or correct the child's KEY values to match an existing parent.

observations.note: The list of parentless groups is hardcoded (copied exactly from python-ags4) rather than derived from the dictionary, because DICT_PGRP does not fully encode checkable parent linkage.

Parent-row resolution matches on the leading columns positionally rather than by the dictionary's named KEY fields. This works for conformant files where KEY fields lead by convention, and matches python-ags4.
An empty KEY cell in a parent row is treated as 'no entry' (permissive) rather than a broken link, matching python-ags4, so blank-keyed parent rows do not trigger orphan errors.

A row whose parent key fields are ALL empty claims no parent, so the parent check is skipped rather than failed - and you get a warning saying so, because a deliberately standalone record (a lab control, an off-site sample) and a key that was blanked by accident look identical from here. The warning does not fail the file. python-ags4 reports nothing at all for these rows.

A file declaring TRAN_AGS "4.0" is ambiguous — there were two 4.0 releases — and the choice shows up here. This validator resolves it to the newer one, which is a strict superset of the older, so no heading is falsely flagged. python-ags4's table picks the older, where PMTL has a different parent, and reports PMTL rows as orphans that this validator does not.

If you validated with a custom dictionary as an OVERLAY, watch for an override warning alongside any finding here. An overlay that re-parents a standard group changes which parent this rule looks for, so rows nobody edited can start reporting as orphans, or stop.

rules.title: Record-Link Delimiter
rules.checks: Checks that the record-link delimiter, declared in TRAN_DLIM (default |), is not empty. Record-Link (RL) fields use this delimiter to separate the target group name from its KEY fields. A finding means TRAN_DLIM was left blank. To fix: the default delimiter | is inserted automatically.

observations.note: A completely absent TRAN_DLIM column is silently allowed (it is not a REQUIRED field); only an empty value triggers this rule. This matches python-ags4.

rules.title: Record-Link Concatenator
rules.checks: Checks that the record-link concatenator, declared in TRAN_RCON (default +), is not empty. This character joins multiple cross-references within a single Record-Link field. A finding means TRAN_RCON was left blank. To fix: the default concatenator + is inserted automatically.

observations.note: An absent TRAN_RCON column is silently allowed (not REQUIRED); only an empty value triggers this rule, matching python-ags4.

rules.title: Record-Link Resolution
rules.checks: Checks that every Record-Link value resolves to exactly one DATA row in the referenced group, using the positional KEY fields. A finding means a link is malformed (wrong format or missing delimiter) or points to a row that does not exist or is ambiguous. To fix: correct the link's group name and KEY values so it resolves to a single target row.

observations.note: Resolution is positional (leading columns) rather than KEY-aware per the dictionary; this works for conformant files and replicates python-ags4.

rules.title: PROJ Group Presence and Row Count
rules.checks: Checks that the file contains a PROJ (project) group with exactly one DATA row. A finding means PROJ is missing or has zero/multiple data rows. To fix: add a PROJ group with a single project record, or reduce it to one row.

observations.note: A zero-row PROJ is reported both here and by Rule 2 (empty group); the spec structure permits this double-report.

A file with no spec-valid (comma-separated, double-quoted) GROUP rows - such as a tab-delimited 'save as text' export, or an empty file - is reported as 'not AGS4' rather than as a list of missing PROJ/TRAN/TYPE/UNIT groups. python-ags4 has no refuse path and instead labels it as merely missing those groups, which is misleading for genuinely non-AGS4 input.

rules.title: TRAN Group Presence and Row Count
rules.checks: Checks that the file contains a TRAN (transaction) group with exactly one DATA row. A finding means TRAN is missing or has zero/multiple data rows. To fix: add a TRAN group with a single transaction record, or reduce it to one row.

observations.note: A zero-row TRAN is reported both here and by Rule 2 (empty group); the spec structure permits this double-report.

TRAN_AGS is not checked for agreement with the dictionary edition being validated against - no AGS rule requires that. The value only selects which standard dictionary is used, falling back to 4.1.1 when it is absent or unrecognised; you can also set the edition explicitly, which overrides the file's declaration.

A TRAN_AGS that is present but not a recognised edition satisfies this rule and still earns a warning, shown by default: the edition could not be matched, so the file was judged against a fallback dictionary its author never declared. python-ags4 reports the same condition only as an FYI you have to opt into. It is a warning and not an error — no rule is broken — so it does not decide the verdict.

rules.title: Unit Definitions
rules.checks: Checks that the file has a UNIT group and that every unit appearing in a UNIT row or in a PU (physical-unit) field is listed in the UNIT group's UNIT_UNIT column. A finding means a unit is used but never defined. To fix: add the missing unit to the UNIT group.

rules.title: Abbreviation Definitions
rules.checks: Checks that when PA (abbreviation) fields are used, every abbreviation is defined in the ABBR group (and a DICT group exists where needed). Fields holding multiple abbreviations are split on the TRAN_RCON concatenator (default +) and each part must be defined separately. A finding means an abbreviation is used but not defined in ABBR. To fix: add the missing abbreviation(s) to the ABBR group.

observations.note: laterite adds an FYI when a PA value is self-declared in the ABBR group but is not a standard abbreviation for its heading (a typo or invented code); python-ags4 has no equivalent check.

rules.title: Data Type Definitions
rules.checks: Checks that the file has a TYPE group and that every type code used in any TYPE row is listed in the TYPE group's TYPE_TYPE column. A finding means a type code is used but never defined. To fix: add the missing type code to the TYPE group.

observations.note: An empty TYPE cell ("") is skipped here rather than flagged, to avoid noise; python-ags4 would flag it. (python-ags4 itself is inconsistent: its Rule 15 skips empty values but its Rule 17 does not.)

rules.title: DICT Group for Non-Standard Names
rules.checks: Checks that if the file uses non-standard GROUP or HEADING names (those flagged by Rule 9), a DICT group is present to define them. A finding means user-defined names are used without a DICT group. To fix: add a DICT group declaring the non-standard groups/headings. With --show-warnings, also flags structural defects in the file's own DICT group (a missing DICT_TYPE/DICT_GRP/DICT_HDNG column, a blank DICT_GRP, or a HEADING row with a blank DICT_HDNG) — a malformed DICT silently degrades downstream checks.

observations.note: This rule fires off Rule 9 (heading) findings only. The spec also mentions non-standard GROUP names, but nothing actually keys off them; this narrow scope matches python-ags4.
laterite adds opt-in WARNING-tier structural validation of the file's own DICT group (the first WARNING-tier producer); python-ags4 only consumes DICT and never validates its structure.

rules.title: GROUP Name Format
rules.checks: Checks that every GROUP name is exactly four uppercase letters (A-Z). A finding means a group name is the wrong length or contains lowercase letters, digits, or symbols. To fix: rename the group to a valid 4-uppercase-letter code.

observations.note: The spec prose loosely permits 'up to 4 characters, uppercase letters and numbers', but this validator enforces the stricter de-facto convention of exactly 4 uppercase letters (matching python-ags4 and the dictionary). All 319 real groups comply, so the stricter rule is safe.

rules.title: HEADING Name Length and Character Set
rules.checks: Checks that every HEADING name is at most 9 characters and uses only uppercase letters, digits, and underscores. A finding means a heading is too long or contains illegal characters; a single bad heading can produce two findings (one for length, one for character set). To fix: shorten the heading and/or remove illegal characters.

rules.title: HEADING Name Structure and Cross-Group Borrowing
rules.checks: Checks that each HEADING follows the AAAA_BBBB pattern: a 4-letter group prefix, an underscore, then a 1-4 character field part (uppercase letters/digits, no further underscore). When a heading borrows another group's prefix (e.g. LOCA_ID used inside SAMP), that heading must actually be defined in the prefix group's dictionary entry. Sanctioned exceptions (SPEC_* and TEST_*) are exempt. A finding means a malformed heading name or an invalid cross-group borrow. To fix: correct the heading to the proper AAAA_BBBB form, or only borrow headings that the source group genuinely defines.

observations.note: The 'field part is at most 4 characters' limit is enforced by python-ags4 but not stated in the spec prose. This validator enforces the same de-facto limit, and all 4,199 real headings obey it.

A heading whose prefix is not a real group can be re-reported by the dictionary-aware sub-checks (19b_2/19b_3) on top of 19b_1/Rule 9. This validator emits two findings for that case (distinguishing 'typo' vs 'wrong placement' fixes) rather than python-ags4's three.

rules.title: File Attachments
rules.checks: Checks that every FILE_FSET value used in any group is defined as a row in the FILE group (and that a FILE group exists when any FILE_FSET is referenced). Optionally, when on-disk checking is enabled, also verifies the sidecar folder layout FILE/<FILE_FSET>/<FILE_NAME> exists next to the .ags file. A finding means a referenced file set is undefined, or (with disk checks on) a referenced attachment is missing on disk. To fix: define the file set in the FILE group, or provide the missing attachment files.

observations.note: On-disk attachment checks are opt-in (off by default); the data-level FILE_FSET check always runs. The corpus QA tool enables disk checks by default, so results there may include missing-file findings you won't see in the default mode.
